abstract: Anthropic surveyed 80,508 Claude.ai personal-account users to understand the perceived economic effects of AI, publishing results in April 2026. One-fifth of respondents voiced concern about economic displacement. Perceived job threat correlated with observed task-level exposure: for every 10-percentage-point increase in exposure, perceived threat rose by 1.3 percentage points, and top-quartile-exposure workers mentioned worry three times as often as bottom-quartile workers. Early-career respondents expressed significantly more concern than senior professionals. The mean productivity rating was 5.1 out of 7 ('substantially more productive'), with only 3% reporting negative or neutral impacts. Among those citing productivity mechanisms, 48% pointed to scope expansion (new tasks they could now do) and 40% to speed improvements. Management occupations (mostly entrepreneurs) and computer/math workers showed the largest gains; scientific and legal professions the mildest. On benefit distribution, 10% of respondents naming a beneficiary said employers or clients captured the surplus; only 60% of early-career workers said they personally benefited versus 80% of senior professionals. A striking U-shaped relationship emerged between reported speedup and perceived job threat: both those slowed by AI and those sped up the most expressed greater anxiety about displacement.
keyFindings: One-fifth of Claude.ai users expressed concern about economic displacement from AI, with top-quartile-exposure workers mentioning worry 3x as often as bottom-quartile workers.
Mean productivity rating of 5.1/7 ('substantially more productive'); productivity gains came from scope expansion (48%) and speed improvements (40%).
Early-career workers were significantly more likely to express displacement concern and less likely to report personal benefit (60% vs 80% for senior professionals).
A U-shaped relationship between speedup and perceived job threat: both those slowed down and those sped up most showed elevated displacement anxiety.
Management and computer/math occupations reported the largest gains; 10% of those identifying a beneficiary said employers/clients capture the surplus rather than workers.
methodology: Survey of 80,508 completed responses from Claude.ai personal-account users, published April 2026. Open-ended responses were classified using Claude-powered classifiers to infer occupations, career stage, and sentiment. The study used Anthropic's observed-exposure metric to correlate task-level AI exposure with perceived threat. Statistical analysis linked exposure quartiles to displacement concern frequency.
qualifiers: Sample is limited to voluntary Claude.ai personal-account users, introducing strong selection bias toward those already using and perceiving value from AI. The population skews toward tech-literate, English-speaking professionals. Occupation and career stage were inferred via AI classifiers rather than self-reported structured data, introducing classification noise. The survey captures perceptions, not actual labor market outcomes. Anthropic's commercial interest in demonstrating AI productivity benefits is a potential framing concern.
